facts.statement: An integrated circuit has many transistors on one chip.
ULSI stands for Ultra Large Scale Integration.
CMOS stands for Complementary Metal Oxide Semiconductor.
CMOS transistors are fast, cheap and low power.
Amorphous Si has no recognizable long-range order.
Amorphous Si has many dangling bonds, and defects, voids and traps.
Amorphous Si is a poor charge conductor.
Poly-Si is made of segments (grains) randomly oriented to each other.
Poly-Si grains range from micron to nm size.
Poly-Si has traps and defects at the grain boundaries, so it is an "average" conductor.
Single-crystal Si is a totally ordered array of atoms with good long-range order and symmetry.
Single-crystal Si has very few defects and traps.
Single-crystal Si is a good conductor if free electrons are present.
The three sketches, left to right, show a random network (amorphous), randomly oriented ordered grains (poly) and one regular grid (single crystal).
Transistors are built on a silicon substrate.
Silicon is a group IV material: 4 electrons to share.
Silicon forms a crystal lattice with bonds to its four nearest neighbours.
The 2D sketch shows silicon atoms sharing electrons in covalent bonds; the 3D sketch shows the cubic unit cell with each atom bonded to four neighbours.
Silicon is a semiconductor.
Pure silicon has no free carriers and conducts poorly.
Adding dopants increases the conductivity.
Group V dopants (e.g. P, As) give an extra electron: n-type.
Group III dopants (e.g. B, Al) leave a missing electron, a hole: p-type.
A junction between p-type and n-type semiconductor forms a diode.
Current flows only in one direction: diode behaviour.
In the diode structure drawing, an n+ layer under the n layer gives low resistance to the metal back contact.
The diode I–V curve shows almost no current in reverse bias and a current rising sharply in forward bias.
The n-region has fixed donor ions with free electrons.
The p-region has fixed acceptor ions with free holes.
Holes diffuse from the p-side (high concentration p_po) to the n-side (low p_no); electrons diffuse the other way.
Near the junction both sides become depleted of majority carriers, exposing the fixed ions.
The region depleted of free carriers on both sides is called the depletion region or space charge layer.
There is an internal electric field from the positive ions to the negative ions, i.e. from the n side to the p side.
In the drawing the p side holds B⁻ acceptor ions and holes, the n side As⁺ donor ions and electrons; the field E0 points from n to p across the space charge region at the metallurgical junction M.
The volume charge density is −eNa in the p-type layer and +eNd in the n-type layer.
Charge neutrality: NaWp = NdWn.
Gauss's theorem: dE/dz = ρ/(εrε0), i.e. −eNa/(εrε0) on the p side and +eNd/(εrε0) on the n side.
εr is the relative permittivity, ε0 the permittivity of free space, ρ the volume charge density, Na and Nd the acceptor and donor densities per unit volume.
Boundary condition: E(−Wp) = E(Wn) = 0.
ρnet is a step (−eNa from −Wp to 0, +eNd from 0 to Wn) and the field is a triangle with its largest magnitude E0 at the junction.
Open circuit: the Fermi level must be uniform through the p- and n-side materials.
At open circuit the potential energy barrier is eV0, the built-in (junction) potential.
Forward bias: the applied voltage drops across the depletion region, the barrier falls to e(V0 − V) and a current flows.
Reverse bias: the barrier rises to e(V0 + Vr).
Under reverse bias, thermal generation of electron–hole pairs in the depletion region gives a small reverse current.
Photo-generation of electron–hole pairs in the depletion region leads to a photocurrent.
In the band diagrams Ec and Ev bend down from p to n; forward bias separates EFn above EFp by eV, reverse bias puts EFn below EFp by eVr.
p-channel is the oldest and simplest technology but is slow, due to the lower mobility of holes.
n-channel is faster than p-channel because electrons have higher mobility than holes.
CMOS (complementary) technology is the prevalent technology at present.
An nMOS transistor has four terminals: gate, source, drain and body.
The gate–oxide–body stack looks like a capacitor: gate and body are conductors, and SiO2 is a very good insulator.
It is called a metal–oxide–semiconductor (MOS) capacitor even though the gate is no longer made of metal.
The nMOS structure drawing shows n-type source and drain in p-type silicon, a gate electrode on silicon dioxide, an n-channel under the gate and metal tracks to source and drain.
The nMOS symbol has gate, source S and drain D, with no circle on the gate.
The nMOS body is commonly tied to ground.
Gate low: the p-type body is at low voltage, the source–body and drain–body diodes are OFF, no current flows: the transistor is OFF.
Gate high: positive charge on the gate attracts negative charge to the body, inverting a channel under the gate to n-type.
With the channel inverted, current flows through n-type silicon from source through the channel to drain: the transistor is ON.
pMOS is like nMOS but with doping and voltages reversed.
The pMOS body is tied to high voltage (VDD).
pMOS: gate low → ON; gate high → OFF.
The circle on the pMOS symbol indicates inverted behaviour.
GND = 0 V.
In the 1980s, VDD = 5 V.
VDD has decreased in modern processes: 3.3, 2.5, 1.8, 1.5, 1.2, 1.0 V, …
VDD fell because high voltage would damage modern tiny transistors, and lower VDD saves power.
The pMOS structure drawing shows p-type source and drain in n-type silicon with a p-channel under a polycrystalline-silicon gate electrode.
MOS transistors can be viewed as electrically controlled switches: the gate voltage controls the path from source to drain.
Switch model, nMOS: g = 0 → OFF (open), g = 1 → ON (closed).
Switch model, pMOS: g = 0 → ON (closed), g = 1 → OFF (open).
Inverter truth table: A = 0 → Y = 1; A = 1 → Y = 0.
CMOS inverter schematic: a pMOS from VDD to Y and an nMOS from Y to GND, both gates driven by A.
VDD stands for the supply voltage.
The inverter symbol is a triangle with a circle (bubble) at the output.
A = 1: the nMOS is ON and the pMOS is OFF, so Y is pulled to GND: Y = 0.
A = 0: the pMOS is ON and the nMOS is OFF, so Y is pulled to VDD: Y = 1.
For each input exactly one of the two inverter transistors is ON and the other OFF.
NAND schematic: two pMOS in parallel from VDD to Y, two nMOS in series from Y to GND.
The NAND symbol is an AND gate with an output bubble, equivalent to an OR gate with bubbles on both inputs.
NAND, A = 0, B = 0: both pMOS ON, both nMOS OFF: Y = 1.
NAND, A = 0, B = 1: the A pMOS is ON (B pMOS OFF) and the series nMOS path is broken by the A nMOS: Y = 1.
NAND, A = 1, B = 0: the B pMOS is ON and the series nMOS path is broken by the B nMOS: Y = 1.
NAND, A = 1, B = 1: both pMOS OFF, both nMOS ON: Y = 0.
NAND truth table: Y = 0 only when A = B = 1.
NOR truth table: Y = 1 only when A = B = 0.
NOR schematic: two pMOS in series from VDD to Y, two nMOS in parallel from Y to GND.
The NOR symbol is an OR gate with an output bubble, equivalent to an AND gate with bubbles on both inputs.
CMOS transistors are fabricated on a silicon wafer.
Lithography is a process similar to a printing press.
On each step, different materials are deposited or etched.
Fabrication is easiest to understand by viewing both the top view and the cross-section of the wafer.
A p-type substrate is typically used for nMOS transistors.
An n-well is required for the body of pMOS transistors.
In the inverter cross-section the nMOS (n+ n+ in the p substrate) is on the left and the pMOS (p+ p+ in the n well) on the right.
The cross-section legend: SiO2, n+ diffusion, p+ diffusion, polysilicon, n well, p substrate, metal1.
A drives both polysilicon gates; Y joins the nMOS and pMOS drains; GND goes to the nMOS source and VDD to the pMOS source.
The substrate must be tied to GND and the n-well to VDD.
Metal on lightly doped semiconductor forms a poor connection called a Schottky diode.
So heavily doped well and substrate contacts (taps) are used.
With taps, the cross-section reads p+ (substrate tap), n+ n+ (nMOS), p+ p+ (pMOS), n+ (well tap).
Transistors and wires are defined by masks.
The cross-section is taken along the dashed line through both transistors and both taps.
Along the dashed line: substrate tap, nMOS, pMOS, well tap, with GND on the left and VDD on the right.
Six masks: n-well, polysilicon, n+ diffusion, p+ diffusion, contact, metal.
Fabrication starts with a blank wafer and builds the inverter from the bottom up.
The first step forms the n-well.
n-well steps: cover the wafer with SiO2, remove it where the n-well goes, implant or diffuse n dopants into the exposed wafer, strip off the SiO2.
Grow SiO2 on top of the Si wafer.
Oxidation: 900–1200 °C with H2O or O2 in an oxidation furnace.
Spin on photoresist.
Photoresist is a light-sensitive organic polymer.
Photoresist softens where exposed to light.
Expose the photoresist through the n-well mask.
Strip off the exposed photoresist.
Etch the oxide with hydrofluoric acid (HF).
HF seeps through skin and eats bone.
HF only attacks oxide where the resist has been exposed (removed).
Strip the remaining photoresist with a mixture of acids called piranha etch.
Stripping is necessary so the resist doesn't melt in the next step.
The n-well is formed by diffusion or ion implantation.
Diffusion: place the wafer in a furnace with arsenic gas and heat until As atoms diffuse into the exposed Si.
Ion implantation: blast the wafer with a beam of As ions.
Ions are blocked by SiO2 and only enter exposed Si.
Strip off the remaining oxide using HF, leaving a bare wafer with an n-well.
Subsequent steps involve a similar series of steps.
Deposit a very thin layer of gate oxide.
Gate oxide is < 20 Å thick: 6–7 atomic layers.
Chemical Vapour Deposition (CVD) of a silicon layer: place the wafer in a furnace with silane gas (SiH4).
CVD forms many small crystals called polysilicon.
Polysilicon is heavily doped to be a good conductor.
The same lithography process patterns the polysilicon.
Use oxide and masking to expose where n+ dopants should be diffused or implanted.
n-diffusion forms the nMOS source, drain and the n-well contact.
Pattern the oxide and form n+ regions.
Self-aligned process: the gate blocks the diffusion.
Polysilicon is better than metal for self-aligned gates because it doesn't melt during later processing.
Historically dopants were diffused; today it is usually ion implantation, but the regions are still called diffusion.
Strip off the oxide to complete the patterning step.
A similar set of steps forms p+ diffusion regions for the pMOS source and drain and the substrate contact.
After the p-diffusion the cross-section reads p+ n+ n+ p+ p+ n+ along the line.
Now the devices must be wired together.
Cover the chip with thick field oxide.
Etch the oxide where contact cuts are needed.
Sputter aluminium over the whole wafer.
Pattern to remove the excess metal, leaving wires.
Chips are specified with a set of masks.
The minimum dimensions of the masks determine transistor size, and hence speed, cost and power.
Feature size f = distance between source and drain, set by the minimum width of polysilicon.
Feature size improves about 30 % every 3 years or so.
Design rules are normalised to feature size and expressed in λ = f/2.
λ = 0.3 µm in a 0.6 µm process.
The simplified design rules are conservative rules to get you started.
Metal1: width 4λ, spacing 4λ.
Metal2: width 4λ, spacing 4λ.
Diffusion: width 4λ, spacing 4λ.
Polysilicon: width 2λ, spacing 3λ.
A polysilicon gate extends 2λ beyond the diffusion it crosses.
Diffusion inside the n-well stays 6λ from the well edge.
Diffusion outside the n-well stays 6λ from the well edge.
Metal1–diffusion contact: the metal surrounds the contact by 1λ.
Metal1–polysilicon contact: the contact is 2λ across.
Metal1–metal2 vias: spacing 3λ.
The slide specifies transistor dimensions as Length / Width.
Minimum transistor size is 4λ / 2λ, sometimes called 1 unit.
In the f = 0.6 µm process the minimum transistor is 0.6 µm (2λ) by 1.2 µm (4λ). The slide words this as "0.6 µm wide, 1.2 µm long"; by slide 46 the 2λ source–drain distance is the channel length.
The slide 48 inverter uses a pMOS of 8/2 (2 units) and an nMOS of 4/2 (1 unit).
In the slide 48 layout VDD runs along the top, GND along the bottom, input A enters on the left and output Y leaves on the right.
MOS transistors are a stack of gate, oxide and silicon.
They can be viewed as electrically controlled switches, and logic gates are built out of switches.
Masks are drawn to specify the layout of transistors.
